claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure consisting of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and is brittle.
A controlled aging heat treatment is proposed to introduce nanoscale precipitates.
The aging treatment will produce nanoscale precipitates distributed within the lamellar microstructure.
The nanoscale precipitates act as dislocation-pinning sites.
The nanoscale precipitates promote dislocation interactions.
Precipitate-mediated pinning, dislocation interactions, and cross-slip reduce dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries.
Reducing dislocation pile-ups mitigates local stress concentrations.
Mitigating local stress concentrations delays microcracking and enhances tensile ductility.
The precipitates increase strength by impeding dislocation motion.
After aging, the alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the untreated starting material.
After aging, the alloy will have greater tensile strength than the untreated starting material.
The intervention is effective only when precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction are optimized to balance strengthening and ductility without causing embrittlement.
Excessive or poorly distributed precipitates can cause embrittlement.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis allows strength to be retained or increased, but the predicted outcome requires increased strength and the falsification rule treats no strength improvement as falsifying. Thus unchanged strength is simultaneously allowed and disallowed.
